activity_context.topic_title: Jordan Canonical Form of a 3x3 Matrix

examples.knowledge_point: Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 3x3 Matrix With Only One Eigenvalue
examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14073225/assets/77995d8d2d70bc6eeb059663883375dbcad8820df3bafc225f854367ee122977.png)

The matrix above has eigenvalues $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=\lambda_3=2.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
examples.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a non-scalar $3 \times 3$ matrix that has the eigenvalue $\lambda=2$ of algebraic multiplicity $3.$ 

As a result, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda=2{:}$

- *Case I.* We may get the single $3 \times 3$ Jordan block $J_3(2).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors $\mathbf v_1, \mathbf v_2$ and $\mathbf v_3$ corresponding to $\lambda=2$ form the following chain:

$$
\mathbf{v}_3 \xrightarrow{A-2I} \mathbf{v}_2 \xrightarrow{A-2I} \mathbf{v}_1 \xrightarrow{A-2I} \mathbf{0}
$$

- *Case II.* We may get a composition of one $2 \times 2$ and one $1 \times 1$ Jordan block, say $J_2(2) {\:\oplus\:} J_1(2).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors $\mathbf v_1, \mathbf v_2$ and $\mathbf v_3$ corresponding to $\lambda=2$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2}\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{3}\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda=2.$

Computing $A-2I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 3 \\ -1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\text{nullity}(A-2I)=1,$ there will be only one eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda=2,$ say, $\mathbf{v}_1.$ So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=2$ form the following chain: 

$$
\mathbf{v}_3 \xrightarrow{A-2 I} \mathbf{v}_2 \xrightarrow{A-2 I} \mathbf{v}_1 \xrightarrow{A-2 I} \mathbf{0}
$$

 

Therefore, we have *case I*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14073225/assets/3fba5b4e0ccc48a2d122b457509e744265b2aa5cfd3625808ebb12fcd421be56.png) 

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

feedback.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 8 & 8 \\ -2 & 5 & 2 \\ -4 & 4 & 7\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=3,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=1.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
feedback.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a $3\times 3$ matrix with the following eigenvalues:

- $\lambda =3$ of algebraic multiplicity $2$

- $\lambda =1$ of algebraic multiplicity $1$

As a result, we have one $1\times 1$ Jordan block ${J}_{1}(1)$ corresponding to $\lambda =1.$
However, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda =3:$

- *Case I.* We may get the single $2\times 2$ Jordan block ${J}_{2}(3).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3$ form the following chain:

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A-3I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-3I\,}{\to }0
$$

- *Case II.* We may get a composition of two $1\times 1$ Jordan blocks, namely ${J}_{1}(3)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(3).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A-3I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A-3I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =3.$

Computing $A-3I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 8 & 8 \\ -2 & 5 & 2 \\ -4 & 4 & 7\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-8 & 8 & 8 \\ -2 & 2 & 2 \\ -4 & 4 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}-8 & 8 & 8 \\ -2 & 2 & 2 \\ -4 & 4 & 4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ -8 & 8 & 8 \\ -4 & 4 & 4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\text{nullity}(A-3I)=2,$ there will be two eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3,$ say, ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}.$ So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3$ form the following chains: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A-3I\,}{\to }0 \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A-3I\,}{\to }0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have *case II*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

$$
{J}_{1}(3)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(3)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(1)=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.
